analysis.body:
The most detailed public accounting of artificial intelligence use inside the United States federal government comes from the Government Accountability Office, which found that twenty of twenty-three major agencies reported roughly 1,200 current and planned AI use cases. Most of those cases were still in the planning phase rather than in production, and only about 200 instances involved AI that agencies were actively using at the time of the review. Reported applications included analyzing drone photography, processing large datasets, identifying information security threats, and targeting scientific specimens for planetary rovers, with NASA and the Department of Commerce reporting the highest number of use cases among the agencies surveyed.

GAO's findings on compliance paint a picture of an implementation effort that is real but incomplete. Ten of the twenty-three agencies had met all AI requirements specific to them, twelve had met only some, and one was exempt. The Office of Management and Budget had not yet developed government-wide guidance on acquiring and using AI, a gap GAO identified as preventing consistent management across agencies. The Office of Personnel Management had not established an updated occupational category for AI workers, and the Office of Science and Technology Policy had not communicated which agencies were expected to fulfill specific requirements. Only the Department of Commerce and the General Services Administration fully implemented the selected requirements GAO examined, with Commerce creating a plan for AI technical standards and GSA establishing an AI Center of Excellence.

Data quality inside agency inventories is itself a problem. Five agencies provided comprehensive information for each reported use case, while the other fifteen had instances of incomplete or inaccurate data. Some inventories omitted required fields such as the AI life cycle stage or releasability status, and two agencies initially submitted uses that were later determined not to be AI at all. GAO concluded that without accurate inventories, the government's ability to manage its AI portfolio will remain constrained. The President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included 1.8 billion dollars for nondefense research and development investment in AI, signaling continued federal financial commitment even as implementation lags.

On the regulatory and legislative side, the volume of activity is substantial. Across all fifty states and U.S. territories, 2,425 AI bills are being tracked, a figure that reflects how quickly legislatures at every level are moving to address the technology. Internationally, Oxford Insights produces a Government AI Readiness Index that scores nearly every country on policy capacity, governance, infrastructure, and public-sector adoption, providing the standard cross-national comparison for how prepared governments are to deploy AI effectively. OECD.AI, the Policy Observatory operated by the OECD, tracks national AI strategies and public-sector initiatives across member and partner countries and has catalogued more than 900 national AI policies and initiatives, with a focus on trustworthy, rights-respecting deployment.

Stanford HAI's annual AI Index tracks government and policy dimensions including legislation counts, national strategy execution, and public-sector procurement, and its 2026 edition notes that frameworks needed to govern and evaluate AI are falling behind the pace of technical capability and adoption. For any organization or government body weighing deployment, the federal experience suggests that the operational and governance infrastructure, accurate inventories, clear acquisition guidance, trained personnel, and defined accountability, matters as much as the technology itself. Agencies that moved to production use cases did so in areas where data inputs were well defined and oversight structures existed; the broader lesson is that AI in government advances more reliably when policy requirements are treated as prerequisites rather than afterthoughts.
